reference.source: Scriver's OMMBID / Nelson Textbook of Paediatrics
clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive disorder caused by biallelic variants in SLC19A3, which encodes the thiamine transporter-2 (hTHTR2)
Impaired thiamine transport into cells produces episodic energy failure in thiamine-dependent tissues, particularly the basal ganglia
Classic childhood presentation is a subacute encephalopathy with confusion, dystonia, dysarthria, seizures and cogwheel rigidity, often triggered by febrile illness
Neuroimaging characteristically shows symmetrical signal change and swelling in the caudate nuclei and putamen, sometimes with cortical involvement
It is one of the few metabolic encephalopathies that is genuinely treatable, with dramatic improvement following high-dose biotin and thiamine supplementation
Delayed treatment or missed crises lead to stepwise accumulation of irreversible basal ganglia injury and fixed dystonia
An infantile Leigh-like variant and an adult Wernicke-like variant broaden the phenotypic spectrum
Lifelong supplementation is required, and interruption can precipitate acute deterioration
reference.pathophysiology: The disease arises from deficient function of thiamine transporter-2 encoded by SLC19A3, which mediates thiamine uptake into cells. Because thiamine (as thiamine pyrophosphate) is an essential cofactor for pyruvate dehydrogenase, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase and transketolase, transporter failure produces intracellular thiamine deficiency and impaired oxidative energy metabolism. The basal ganglia, with high metabolic demand, are especially vulnerable, so metabolic stress such as fever or fasting precipitates acute energy crises with cytotoxic oedema and neuronal injury. Supraphysiological biotin and thiamine are thought to drive residual transporter activity and alternative uptake pathways, restoring intracellular thiamine.
additionalDifferentials: Leigh syndrome and other mitochondrial encephalopathies
Juvenile Huntington disease and other inherited dystonias
additionalInvestigations: Brain MRI seeking symmetrical caudate and putaminal signal change with swelling
Molecular genetic testing of SLC19A3 to confirm the diagnosis
Cerebrospinal fluid and plasma metabolic screen to exclude mimics
Blood lactate and pyruvate to assess for mitochondrial or energy-metabolism disease
A monitored therapeutic trial of biotin and thiamine with clinical and radiological response
redFlags: Subacute encephalopathy with dystonia and rigidity following a febrile illness
Rapid neurological deterioration during intercurrent illness or fasting
Symmetrical basal ganglia signal change on imaging
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends critically on how early treatment begins; when high-dose biotin and thiamine are started promptly, recovery from acute crises can be near-complete. Delayed or missed episodes cause cumulative basal ganglia damage with residual dystonia, dysarthria and cognitive impairment.
pitfalls: Missing a treatable diagnosis and managing the child only as viral or autoimmune encephalitis
Stopping supplementation once the child improves, precipitating relapse
Failing to escalate treatment urgently during febrile crises
Overlooking atypical infantile or adult-onset presentations
references: Scriver's Online Metabolic and Molecular Bases of Inherited Disease
